title: Ezra the Scribe and the King's Letter
summary: Nearly sixty years after the temple's completion, Ezra, a priest descended from Aaron and a scribe skilled in the law of Moses, travels from Babylon to Jerusalem with a group of returnees in the seventh year of King Artaxerxes. The chapter gives his genealogy, his purpose, and the full text of the king's letter authorizing him to lead volunteers, carry gifts for the temple, draw on royal funds, and teach and enforce the law of God west of the Euphrates. Ezra responds with a blessing of the LORD who moved the king's heart.
story: Chapter 6 ended with the temple finished in 515 BC. Chapter 7 opens with the words many years later, and the gap is about fifty-seven years, during which the story of Esther (set under Xerxes) takes place elsewhere in the empire. The first half of Ezra was about rebuilding the house of God. The second half is about rebuilding the people around the law of God, and Ezra himself is the man for that work. Only now, in chapter 7, does the book's title character appear. His arrival shifts the book's focus from stones to Scripture, and at verse 27 the voice shifts too: from here through chapter 9 Ezra speaks in the first person, in what scholars call the Ezra Memoir. The next chapter tells his trip in detail, and chapters 9 and 10 show the crisis he faced on arrival.
historical:
The traditional and still most widely held view identifies the king as Artaxerxes I (465-424 BC), whose seventh year was 458 BC. On that reckoning Ezra came thirteen years before Nehemiah. Some scholars argue for Artaxerxes II (404-358 BC), which would date Ezra to 398 BC, after Nehemiah; a few propose emending the text to the thirty-seventh year of Artaxerxes I, about 428 BC. The debate turns on the relationship between Ezra and Nehemiah in Nehemiah 8 and 12 and on the names of high priests in the period.

The king's letter (verses 12-26) fits known Persian practice. Persian kings supported local temples and sometimes authorized the codification of local laws. An Egyptian official named Udjahorresnet recorded on his statue, now in the Vatican Museums, that Darius I sent him back to Egypt to restore an institution of learning at Sais, a close parallel to a Persian king sending a learned subject home with royal backing. The seven counselors of verse 14 recall the seven nobles of Persia and Media in Esther 1:14. Whether Ezra's title of scribe was also an official Persian office, as some scholars have suggested, is debated.
cultural:
A scribe (sopher) in the ancient world was more than a copyist. Scribes were trained in writing, law, and administration and served temples and royal courts. In Ezra's case the word takes on a new meaning: he is a scribe of the law of Moses, a scholar of Scripture whose skill is in understanding and teaching it. The later Jewish office of the scribe, and the scribes who appear in the Gospels, look back to this figure. Ezra's priestly genealogy (verses 1-5) traces his line back to Aaron; it is abridged, skipping several generations known from 1 Chronicles 6:3-15, which was a common practice in ancient genealogies. His father is named as Seraiah, the chief priest executed by the Babylonians in 587 or 586 BC (2 Kings 25:18-21); since that was more than a century before Ezra's arrival, son here must mean descendant.

The trip from Babylon to Jerusalem, following the Euphrates northwest and then turning south, covered roughly 900 miles and took four months (verses 8-9). The gifts Ezra carried, the exemption of temple personnel from royal taxes, and the king's concern that God's wrath not fall on his realm (verse 23) reflect the ancient conviction that honoring a people's god protected the empire.
literary: The chapter has three parts: Ezra's introduction in Hebrew (verses 1-11), Artaxerxes' letter in Aramaic (verses 12-26), and Ezra's own blessing in Hebrew (verses 27-28), where the first-person voice begins. The introduction is built around a repeated phrase: the hand of the LORD his God was upon him (verses 6, 9, and 28). The central verse is verse 10, which gives the reason God's hand was on Ezra: “Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel.” The order matters. Study leads to practice, and practice to teaching. The king's letter uses the Persian loanword dat for law, placing the law of God and the law of the king side by side in verse 26.

outline.t: Ezra comes to Jerusalem, devoted to the law
Artaxerxes' letter: volunteers, gifts, and temple funds
Orders to the treasurers and tax exemption for temple servants
Ezra's authority to appoint judges and teach the law
Ezra blesses the LORD for the king's favor

doctrines.note: Ezra is defined by his devotion to the law the LORD had given through Moses. The chapter treats Scripture as God's own gift, to be studied, obeyed, and taught, and it marks the rise of a community centered on the written word.

The king grants Ezra all he asks because the hand of the LORD was upon him, and Ezra blesses God for putting it into the king's heart to honor the temple. God's favor works through a pagan king's generosity.

The law of Moses is presented not as a burden but as the charter of the community's life. Ezra's commission is to teach it to those who do not know it and to see it upheld, in both worship and justice.

words.note: Darash, to seek, inquire, or study. It is used of seeking God in prayer and of consulting a prophet, and here in verse 10 of Ezra setting his heart to seek, that is to study, the law of the LORD. Later Jewish tradition drew its word midrash, interpretation of Scripture, from this root. Study here is a form of seeking God.

Sopher, scribe or secretary. It can name a royal official in charge of documents, like Shimshai in chapter 4. Applied to Ezra, it gains a new sense: a scribe skilled in the law of Moses, an expert interpreter and teacher of Scripture, the forerunner of the scribes of later Judaism.

Yad, hand, used here for power and favor. The refrain that the hand of the LORD was upon Ezra (verses 6, 9, 28) is the book's way of describing God's active, protective guidance through ordinary events: a king's goodwill, a safe road, the courage to gather others.

Dat, law or decree, a Persian loanword used in the Aramaic letter. The law of your God and the law of the king appear together in verse 26, reflecting how the Persian empire gave legal force to the religious laws of its peoples. In Esther the same word is used for the laws of the Medes and Persians.

christ: Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law sent to restore God's people, belongs to a line of figures whose work anticipates something greater. The scribes of the Gospels, who looked back to Ezra, were often Jesus' opponents, yet Jesus spoke of every scribe trained for the kingdom of heaven as bringing out treasures new and old (Matthew 13:52). The pattern of verse 10, study and practice and teaching, is also the pattern of Jesus' own ministry, which the Gospels describe as teaching with authority and doing what he taught. Jesus said he came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matthew 5:17). The link is thematic: Ezra shows what devotion to God's word looks like in a human servant, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the one in whom that word is perfectly lived and fully revealed.
questions: Ezra set his heart to study the law, to practice it, and to teach it, in that order. Which of these three comes easiest to you, and which do you tend to skip?
Ezra saw God's hand in the favor of a foreign king. Where might you be overlooking God's work in the ordinary decisions of people around you?
The chapter places the law of God and the law of the king side by side. How should a believer relate faithfulness to God with obedience to human governments?
